Ceramic CNC Machining Process Overview What Types of Ceramics Are Commonly CNC Machined and How to Choose the Right One How Engineers Actually Choose the Right Ceramic Material Key CNC Machining Parameters for Ceramics Applications, Advantages & Practical Tips Conclusion FAQ Ceramic CNC Machining: Key Process, Parameters & Tips What Is Ceramic CNC Machining? CNC machine using a diamond tool to cut a ceramic part in a clean industrial workshop. Ceramic CNC machining is the process of cutting, shaping, and finishing advanced ceramics using precision CNC equipment. You see it everywhere high heat, electrical insulation, or extreme wear resistance is required, aerospace seals, semiconductor fixtures, medical implants, cutting tools, all the usual suspects. Ceramics behave nothing like metals or plastics during machining. They're incredibly hard, brittle, and completely unforgiving. Push the feed rate a little too much or hit the wrong vibration zone, and the part doesn't deform, it just cracks. That's why the process depends so heavily on rigid setups, diamond tooling, and predictable toolpaths. You'll see two very different approaches in the industry: • Green machining: This happens before sintering, when the ceramic is still in its “chalk-like” pre-fired state. It's softer, easier to cut, and far less risky. Most shops try to do as much as possible at this stage because it saves tools, time, and headache. • Sintered machining: Once the ceramic is fired, it becomes extremely hard, often harder than tool steels. Any post-sintering cuts require diamond tooling, slow speeds, and laser-focused process control. It's used only when the part needs tight tolerances that can't be held through shrinkage. Both routes fall under ceramic CNC machining , but the workflow, cost, and tool wear are totally different. The trick is choosing the right stage to machine so you're not fighting the material unnecessarily. Ceramic CNC Machining Process Overview CNC machining ceramic parts is a very “controlled chaos” kind of operation. The machines look similar to what you'd use for aluminum or steel, but the setup is a different universe. You need a rigid, high-speed CNC machine with a clean, vibration-free spindle. Ceramics don't like chatter, even a hint of it can spider-crack an otherwise perfect part. Most shops run 40,000–60,000 RPM spindles for fine features, with super-stable bearings and balanced tool holders to keep everything smooth. Cutting Tools You Can Actually Use Ceramics don't care about your usual end mills. They eat carbide for breakfast. So you'll see two tool families: Diamond tools (PCD/diamond-coated): The go-to option for sintered ceramics. They're expensive, but they stay sharp long enough to make financial sense. Carbide tools: Used mainly for green machining when the material still cuts like a dense chalk. Once it's fired, carbide taps out instantly. Coolant, Dust & Heat Control Every cut throws off ultra-fine ceramic dust, abrasive, airborne, and terrible for lungs and machines. So you'll see one of these setups: Flood coolant for sintered parts to keep temperatures steady and capture dust. Dry machining with vacuum extraction for green-state parts, where coolant can cause swelling or instability. Heat management is everything. One tiny hot spot and the outer layer microfractures. Toolpaths Built for Ceramics No aggressive plunging. No “send it” roughing passes. Ceramics want: Shallow stepdowns Light radial engagement Continuous, stable toolpaths (adaptive clearing with gentle entry) Minimal re-entry to avoid edge chipping Programmers often treat the part like glass: slow, steady, predictable motion beats raw MRR every time. Pre- and Post-Processing Steps Ceramic machining usually wraps into a bigger workflow: Pre-machining: Degassing, green machining, debinding, and allowing shrinkage planning. Post-machining: Sintering, diamond grinding, polishing, lapping, or laser trimming for final tolerances. Some shops even do a final surface seal or inspection under polarized light to catch subsurface cracks. What Types of Ceramics Are Commonly CNC Machined and How to Choose the Right One Close-up studio photo of different engineering ceramics, alumina, zirconia, Macor, aluminum nitride, and glass-ceramic, displayed as machined samples. Ceramics aren't a single category. They behave wildly differently once you put a tool into them. Some cut like chalk, some chip if you even look at them wrong, and some will eat your tooling budget alive. Picking the right material upfront saves you from cracked parts, impossible tolerances, or heat-related failure later. Below are the materials you'll see most often in CNC ceramic work, and how engineers usually decide between them. Macor (Machinable Glass Ceramic) Macor is the material everyone starts with because it behaves like a stiff engineering plastic in the spindle. You can cut it dry, hold fine features, and avoid the nightmare of diamond-tool-only machining. Best for: prototypes, insulating fixtures, jigs, electrical components. Why choose it: excellent machinability, stable at high temperature, good dielectric strength. Watch out: lower strength and brittleness compared to technical ceramics. Alumina Ceramics (Al₂O₃) This is the workhorse. Once sintered, it's extremely hard, abrasion resistant, and unforgiving. Expect to use diamond tooling and careful feeds. Best for: wear components, medical devices, precision guides, structural insulators. Why choose it: high hardness, corrosion resistance, excellent electrical insulation. Watch out: poor machinability once fully fired; machining green alumina is usually cheaper. Aluminum Nitride (AlN) If thermal management matters, this material jumps to the top of the list. Best for: heat spreaders, power electronics, semiconductor tooling. Why choose it: extremely high thermal conductivity, stable at high temperatures. Watch out: brittle; needs conservative toolpaths and good dust extraction. Graphite Ceramics Graphite machines beautifully, almost too easily. But it's messy. Best for: EDM electrodes, high-temp fixtures, furnace parts. Why choose it: excellent thermal resistance, clean cuts, low tool wear. Watch out: dust everywhere; requires sealed machines or strong vacuum systems. Glass & Glass-Ceramics Used when transparency or precise dielectric behavior is part of the design. Best for: optics, sensor housings, precision labware. Why choose it: stable under heat, dimensionally predictable. Watch out: chipping during edge finishing; requires gentle tool entry/exit. If you're exploring non-ceramic options too, our Plastic CNC Machining Guide helps compare machinability, thermal behavior, and cost. If you also need CNC machining for aluminum, stainless steel, copper, or other metals, JLCCNC can help . We offer fast quoting, stable tolerances, and reliable global delivery—ideal for both prototypes and production. How Engineers Actually Choose the Right Ceramic Material Engineer examining different ceramic materials, laid out on a workstation with calipers, labeled samples, and material datasheets When you’re working with CNC machining ceramic , the decision normally hinges on these factors: Thermal Conductivity If the part handles heat, power circuits, LEDs, laser modules, Aluminum Nitride almost always wins. Alumina works when you need insulation instead of heat flow. Wear Resistance For anything sliding, rotating, or rubbing, fired alumina is the safest choice. Zirconia (if included later) is another tough option. Toughness (Resistance to Cracking) Ceramics are inherently brittle, but some are less drama-prone than others. Tougher: zirconia, silicon nitride (optional if you add later) Brittle: glass, fired alumina For parts with thin walls or slots, machinable ceramics like Macor avoid fracture issues. Precision & Surface Finish Needs Macor gives the easiest path to fine features. Alumina and AlN need diamond tooling and careful stepdowns to hit smooth Ra values. If the part must be optically clean, glass ceramics are the go-to. Key CNC Machining Parameters for Ceramics Ceramics don't forgive sloppy parameters. If your feeds or depths get even a little aggressive, the part lets you know instantly, usually by snapping, chipping, or exploding into expensive confetti. Below are the CNC machining parameters for ceramics that actually matter in real shops. Cutting Speed Recommendations Ceramics hate heat spikes, and they punish unstable chip loads. Speeds are usually far lower than metals: Diamond tools (PCD/diamond-coated): 120–350 m/min depending on material hardness Carbide tools: only for machinable ceramics like Macor, usually 30–60 m/min The rule of thumb: start on the conservative end and creep upward only if the surface finish can handle it. Feed Rate & Depth of Cut “Shave,” not “cut.” Feed rate: light, steady, predictable. Something in the 5–30 mm/min range is common for fired alumina and AlN. Depth of cut: tiny. Many shops run 0.01–0.05 mm stepdowns on hard ceramics. Macor is the exception, you can run it like a fragile engineering plastic, but even then, shallow passes help avoid micro-cracking. Managing Tool Wear & Preventing Tool Fracture Diamond tools don't chip often, but they wear gradually and invisibly . Performance drops before the tool looks dull. Watch for: rising spindle load sudden surface roughness faint “screeching” or whitening on the cut path Switch tools early; it's cheaper than scrapping a part that took two hours to rough. Fixturing Considerations Ceramics demand full support. They don't bend, they just break. Use soft jaws or vacuum fixtures to distribute load evenly. Avoid point clamps or step clamps unless the part has thick walls. When machining green ceramic, you can be a little looser; once sintered, treat it like glass. How to Reduce Cracks, Chipping & Breakage This is where most projects fail. A few habits change everything: Gentle entry/exit moves: ramp or helix instead of plunging. Constant tool engagement: avoid sudden re-cuts or interrupted edges. Mist cooling or air blasts: enough to carry dust and cool the tool without thermal shocking the ceramic. High-frequency stepovers: lots of small, consistent bites instead of diving deep. Check for internal stress: sintered ceramics can contain residual tension, rough with very light passes first to relieve it. Applications, Advantages & Practical Tips Ceramic CNC machining lives in the kind of industries where failure isn't allowed, semiconductor fabs, aerospace systems, high-temp electrical components, and anything that deals with corrosive chemicals or ridiculous heat. The parts tend to be small, precise, and hellishly difficult to replace once installed, which is why ceramic CNC machining remains the go-to route for many engineers. Common Ceramic CNC Parts Across industries, you'll see a few recurring components: Semiconductor: wafer handling arms, probe housings, insulating fixtures, plasma-resistant parts Aerospace: thermal barrier inserts, fuel-system insulators, high-stability brackets Medical: bio-inert guides, implant tooling components, imaging alignment blocks General industrial: wear plates, chemical-resistant pump components, high-precision metrology fixtures These parts benefit from the dimensional accuracy that grinding or casting simply can't hit. When CNC Machining Is Better Than Grinding or Laser Processing Grinding is the gold standard for surface finish, but it's slow and doesn't scale well for anything with complex geometry. Laser machining works for thin sections or micro-features, but the heat input can leave micro-cracks in some ceramics. CNC machining wins when you need: deep pockets or multi-axis surfaces tight tolerances on complex 3D shapes clean edges without heat-affected zones rapid iteration before sintering (green machining) If you're dealing with fired alumina or zirconia, a hybrid approach, CNC roughing + grinding finish passes , is pretty standard in industry. Practical Machining Tips for High-Quality Ceramic Parts A few habits separate shops that get repeat ceramic work from those that shatter parts for a week and give up: Keep your cutter load boringly stable. No sudden plunges, no re-cuts, no surprise tool engagement. Use diamond tools whenever possible. Carbide only survives on softer ceramics. Mist cooling + dust evacuation > flooding. You don't want thermal shock or slurry buildup. Plan your toolpath around fragility. Inside corners, thin ribs, and sharp transitions need extremely gentle entry/exit moves. Machine green whenever the project allows. You get way more freedom before sintering. If your part is sintered and you're working with wall thicknesses under 1 mm, expect scrap. That's just the reality of the material. Conclusion Ceramic CNC machining isn't something you brute-force. It rewards slow, deliberate setups and tools that stay sharp longer than your patience. When done right, though, you get components that survive heat, abrasion, chemicals, and electrical stress far better than metals or plastics. If you want your ceramic part prototyped or produced without the guesswork, JLCCNC can machine most grades, from Macor to alumina to AlN, with tight tolerances and clean edges FAQ 1. Which ceramics are easiest to CNC machine? Macor and machinable glass ceramics are by far the easiest. Alumina and zirconia are much harder and require diamond tooling. 2. Can you machine sintered ceramics? Yes, but expect tiny depths of cut and slow feeds. Sintered material behaves more like glass than metal. 3. Do ceramics require coolant during CNC machining? Usually a light mist or air blast is enough. Flood coolant risks thermal shock. 4. Is ceramic CNC machining expensive? Compared to aluminum or plastics, yes. The tools, time, and scrap risk drive up cost. 5. When is green machining better? Any time the design allows it. You can remove material faster and with far fewer breakages before sintering. That's just the reality of the material. Conclusion Ceramic CNC machining isn't something you brute-force. It rewards slow, deliberate setups and tools that stay sharp longer than your patience. When done right, though, you get components that survive heat, abrasion, chemicals, and electrical stress far better than metals or plastics. If you want your ceramic part prototyped or produced without the guesswork, JLCCNC can machine most grades, from Macor to alumina to AlN, with tight tolerances and clean edges FAQ 1. Which ceramics are easiest to CNC machine? Macor and machinable glass ceramics are by far the easiest. Alumina and zirconia are much harder and require diamond tooling. 2. Can you machine sintered ceramics? Yes, but expect tiny depths of cut and slow feeds. Sintered material behaves more like glass than metal. 3. Do ceramics require coolant during CNC machining? Usually a light mist or air blast is enough. Flood coolant risks thermal shock. 4. Is ceramic CNC machining expensive? Compared to aluminum or plastics, yes. The tools, time, and scrap risk drive up cost. 5. When is green machining better? Any time the design allows it. You can remove material faster and with far fewer breakages before sintering. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals CNC Meets 3D Printing Smarter Stainless Steel Manufacturing for Aerospace, Medical & More Published May 15, 2025, updated May 15, 2025 5 min In the high-end manufacturing industry, the complex structure of stainless steel parts and high-precision demand for the traditional manufacturing model presents a great challenge. The synergistic application of CNC machining and metal 3D printing is through the “near-net shaping + precision machining” hybrid manufacturing strategy, breakthrough technology bottlenecks, to achieve the double optimization of cost and efficiency. This article will analyze the stainless steel hybrid manufacturing technology path, core advantages and industry applications. I. Stainless steel hybrid manufacturing technology logic: 3D printing and CNC synergy optimization 1. Complementary technical characteristics 3D printing (SLM/DMLS) : The use of laser melting stainless steel powder layer by layer, can be shaped into complex cavities, lattice structure and other traditional processes difficult to achieve the geometry, the material utilization rate of up to 95%. CNC Machining: Precision cutting of 3D printed blanks through 5-axis linkage technology, surface roughness up to Ra0.4μm, tolerance control ±0.01mm, to meet the needs of high-precision assembly. 2. Hybrid manufacturing process Near-net-molding stage: Printing stainless steel blanks based on SLM technology, retaining critical area allowance (0.1-0.3mm) to reduce material waste. Precision machining stage: Five-axis CNC machine tool finishes critical areas such as mating surfaces, threaded holes, etc. to eliminate print layer pattern and optimize surface quality. Post-processing integration: Sandblasting, electrolytic polishing and other processes to enhance corrosion resistance, anodizing to enhance surface hardness (HV ≥ 800). II. 4 Core Advantages of Hybrid Manufacturing 1. Cost reduction: material and man-hours double optimization Case: an aerospace engine bracket using hybrid manufacturing, 3D printing weight reduction of 40%, CNC machining only 20% of the traditional labor hours, total cost reduction of 35%, complex parts processing cycle shortened by 50%. 2. Integrated molding of complex structures Technological breakthroughs: Conformal Cooling Runner: 3D printing embedded spiral water path, CNC finishing sealing surface, mold life increased by 3 times. Skeletonization and lightweighting: Titanium-stainless steel composite structure, unchanged strength and 50% weight reduction. 3. Synergistic improvement of precision and performance Surface quality: Hybrid manufacturing part surface roughness optimized from Ra30μm in SLM to Ra0.4μm to meet medical device implantation requirements. Mechanical properties: Tensile strength is increased by 15% (e.g. 17-4PH up to 1200MPa) through CNC elimination of printing residual stresses. 4. Small batch agile production Support 1-piece ordering, from design to delivery in as fast as 3 days (traditional mold manufacturing takes more than 30 days). III. Stainless steel hybrid manufacturing of the five innovative application direction 1. Semiconductor equipment precision components Demand: wafer transfer robotic arm needs to be both lightweight (weight reduction of 30%) and corrosion resistance (resistant to strong acid environment). Solution: 316L stainless steel 3D printed honeycomb sandwich structure, CNC finishing gripping surface, surface roughness up to Ra0.2μm, precision ± 0.005mm, life expectancy increased by 3 times. Value: a lithography manufacturer through the program, wafer transfer speed increased by 15%, maintenance cycle extended to 12 months. 2. Functional integration of energy equipment Hydrogen energy field: Fuel cell bipolar plate adopts 3D printing runner + CNC sealing surface processing, hydrogen permeability is reduced to 0.01cm³/min, and mass production cost is reduced by 40%. Nuclear energy field: nuclear reactor cooling tube by SLM molding inner wall spiral groove, 5-axis CNC polishing to Ra0.1μm, heat exchange efficiency increased by 25%. 3. Smart hardware structural innovation Consumer electronics: folding screen cell phone hinges are manufactured with 17-4PH stainless steel hybrid, realizing 0.01mm-level assembly tolerance and opening and closing life of over 500,000 times. Robot joints: Many robot joints use 3D-printed bionic bone structure, and then use CNC machining their bearing mating surfaces, so that the dynamic load capacity of the robot joints is increased by 30% and the weight is reduced by 40%. 4. Green Circular Economy Practices Waste material regeneration: remelting stainless steel scraps from CNC machining into 3D printing powder, material utilization rate increased from 20% to 95%. Low-carbon process: hybrid manufacturing energy consumption is 60% lower than traditional casting, and an enterprise reduces carbon emissions by 1,200 tons per year. IV. 3 Implementation Strategies for Hybrid Manufacturing 1. Material and process matching Material selection: Prioritize 316L or 17-4PH stainless steel with strong SLM suitability to avoid work hardening. Parameter synergy: Printing layer thickness: 20-40μm (balance efficiency and surface quality). Cutting parameters: carbide tool line speed 80-120m/min, feed 0.05mm/tooth. 2. Digital full-process management Software integration: UG/NX and other platforms to achieve “modeling - slicing - machining path” integrated programming, reducing data conversion errors. Intelligent inspection: Combination of coordinate measurement (CMM) and CT scanning ensures that the detection rate of internal defects is >99%. 3. Economic assessment model Cost formula: Total Cost = Printing Cost (Material + Energy) + CNC Finishing Cost (Man-hour + Tool) When the complexity of the part > 60%, the cost of the hybrid program is lower than pure CNC machining. V. Contact JLCCNC today to unlock the infinite possibilities of stainless steel parts manufacturing! Introduction: The importance of understanding CNC machining misconceptions CNC (Computer Numerical Control) machining has become an integral part of the modern manufacturing industry and is widely used in a variety of fields due to its high accuracy and efficiency. From automotive to aerospace, from medical to electronics, CNC machining technology provides manufacturers with a wealth of machining solutions. However, in practice, some common misconceptions often affect machining accuracy, productivity and the quality of the final product. This article will explore these common misconceptions and provide solutions to help manufacturers avoid problems that may arise in CNC machining, and enhance production levels. II. Common misconceptions about CNC machining 1. Excessive pursuit of machining accuracy In many CNC machining projects, the excessive pursuit of very high precision often leads to unnecessary machining difficulties and cost increases. While high-precision machining is critical in certain demanding industries, in many cases, overly tight tolerance requirements not only increase manufacturing time, but can also lead to rapid tool wear. How to avoid it: Set tolerances appropriately and consider the actual use of the part. If the function of the part does not require extreme accuracy, tolerances can be relaxed appropriately, reducing machining costs and increasing productivity. Example: For example, in the mass production of automotive parts, excessive pursuit of micron-level tolerances may lead to unnecessary machining processes. By setting tolerances to a reasonable range, the functionality of the part can be ensured and significant savings in machining time and cost can be achieved. 2. Inappropriate material selection Selection of unsuitable materials often leads to increased machining difficulty and even increased tool wear during machining, reducing productivity. Material selection is critical to the CNC machining process, and the hardness, toughness, thermal conductivity and wear resistance of different materials have a significant impact on the machining process. How to avoid: Select materials based on the functional requirements, mechanical properties and machining characteristics of the part. Designers should communicate with CNC machining suppliers to understand the impact of material properties on the machining process and make a reasonable choice. Example: For example, aluminium alloys are suitable for parts with lightweight requirements, but for parts that need to withstand large mechanical loads, using steel or titanium alloys may be more appropriate. Selecting materials according to different needs can effectively avoid difficulties and mistakes in machining. 3. Neglect tool selection and maintenance Tool selection and maintenance for CNC machining is critical. Inappropriate tool selection may lead to errors in the machining process, or even cause parts to be scrapped. Tool wear, deformation and other problems are also common misconceptions in machining. How to avoid: Select the appropriate tool according to the machining material, part shape and machining accuracy requirements, and regularly check the wear of the tool. Replace the tool in time to maintain the sharpness of the tool to ensure the smoothness of the machining process. EDM vs Drilling: The Core Differences When to Use EDM Hole Drilling When to Use Conventional CNC Drilling EDM Holes vs Drilled Holes: What About Quality? Limitations to Consider EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way Drilling a hole sounds simple, until you need to do it with extreme precision, into hardened materials, or to microscopic depths. That’s when you start comparing EDM hole drilling and conventional CNC drilling side by side. While both are designed to create holes, their technologies, capabilities, and ideal use cases couldn’t be more different. So, which method should you choose for your next project? Let’s dig in. What Is EDM Hole Drilling? EDM (Electrical Discharge Machining) hole drilling , also called hole popping EDM or EDM deep hole drilling , uses electrical sparks to erode material. Instead of a rotating drill bit, it uses a tubular electrode and dielectric fluid to remove metal through high-frequency discharges. It’s a non-contact process, meaning the tool doesn’t make direct physical contact with the material during machining. The result? It can drill extremely precise, burr-free holes even in hardened steel, carbides, or exotic alloys . What Is Conventional CNC Hole Drilling? CNC hole drilling uses rotating cutting tools<dynamic-value> twist drills or end mills, to cut into material. It's what most people imagine when they think about machining a hole. From high-speed spindles to peck drilling cycles, CNC machines are versatile and fast, especially when you're working with softer materials or mass production. But it’s still a contact-based process , and precision can degrade with wear, heat, or vibration. EDM vs Drilling: The Core Differences Feature EDM Hole Drilling CNC Drilling Material Type Conductive materials only (e.g., steel, titanium) Any machinable material Tool Contact No physical contact Direct contact via tool Hole Size Micro to medium (0.1 mm to 6 mm) Wide range (0.5 mm to 50+ mm) Tolerance Extremely tight (±0.002 mm possible) Moderate (±0.05 mm typical) Hole Depth Excellent for deep, narrow holes (30:1+ depth-to-diameter) Limited by tool rigidity and chip evacuation Speed Slower Faster for larger holes Surface Finish Very smooth, no burrs May require deburring or finishing Tool Wear Minimal due to no mechanical contact High, especially in hard materials Are you unsure about which process is right for your metal part? We can help you choose the most precise and cost-effective method for your job. Get a free quote here and let's make your design manufacturable. When to Use EDM Hole Drilling The EDM hole drilling process shines in high-precision, small-diameter, deep-hole situations, especially where conventional drilling fails or causes tool breakage. Use cases include: ● Turbine blades (for cooling holes) ● Fuel injector nozzles ● Aerospace components ● Medical devices requiring micro holes ● Hard tool steels or materials like Inconel and titanium Also, EDM is ideal when you need starter holes for wire EDM , which conventional tools can’t drill due to hardness or geometry. When to Use Conventional CNC Drilling For general-purpose hole making in aluminum, plastics, or mild steel, CNC hole drilling is faster and more cost-effective. Use cases include: ● Bolt holes, pilot holes, tapped holes ● Large hole drilling in brackets or frames ● Machining production parts in batches ● Applications where tight tolerance is not critical And yes, to answer a common question, can a CNC machine drill holes? Absolutely. In fact, it’s one of the most common operations in any CNC shop. EDM Holes vs Drilled Holes: What About Quality? EDM holes tend to be cleaner and burr-free straight off the machine. Their surface finish is smoother, with no mechanical stress or deformation around the hole. This makes them ideal for critical applications where dimensional stability and fatigue resistance matter. CNC-drilled holes, on the other hand, often need secondary processes , like deburring or reaming, to meet similar tolerances and finishes, especially in small diameters or deep holes. Limitations to Consider While EDM hole drilling offers unmatched precision, it’s not ideal for every scenario . ● It can’t be used on non-conductive materials (like plastic or glass). ● It’s relatively slow for large-diameter holes. ● Machines and electrodes are more expensive and require specialized operators. Conversely, CNC drilling tools wear faster in hardened materials, and the deeper you go, the higher the risk of tool deflection, chatter, or breakage . EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? A dedicated hole drilling EDM machine is typically compact, automated, and capable of producing holes as small as 0.1 mm in tough metals. Many come with automatic electrode changers and multi-axis positioning. For shops working with aerospace, mold making, or die sinking, having one on the floor is a game-changer for precision parts. Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way If you're prototyping intricate components or producing parts where one imperfect hole can ruin the entire build , go for EDM. But if you’re running production batches, drilling aluminum brackets, or cutting costs, CNC drilling is often more practical. Choose the Right Tool for the Hole Not every hole is created equal, and neither are the tools that make them. Whether you choose EDM hole drilling for ultra-precision or CNC hole drilling for speed and efficiency, understanding their strengths is the first step toward better manufacturing outcomes. If you’re unsure what your application calls for, talk to your machinist, or even better, partner with a shop that offers both options . How the Face Milling Process Works Common Face Milling Tools Types of Face Milling Operations Best Practices for Cleaner Face Milling Master the Cut Before You Hit Cycle Start Face milling doesn’t get the spotlight much, but it’s one of those workhorse processes that keeps machining shops running smooth. If you’ve ever needed a flat surface that’s actually flat , you’ve relied on it, whether you realized it or not. So what exactly is face milling? Think of it as the process behind every perfectly squared metal block, every smooth aluminum plate, every clean surface that just feels right. It’s precise, fast, and oddly satisfying to watch. But it’s not just about spinning a tool across some metal. The cutter design, tool path, speeds, and setup all play a role in getting that crisp finish without wrecking your inserts or your workpiece. In this guide, we’re breaking down how face milling works, what tools you’ll need, the types of operations involved, and a few tips that’ll save your cutters, and your sanity. What Is Face Milling? (istock) Face milling is one of the most common, and most essential, processes in the machining world. It’s all about cutting a flat surface perpendicular to the tool’s axis, usually with a wide face mill cutter that skims across the top of the material. The result? A smooth, level finish that’s ready for the next operation. Unlike side milling , which cuts along the edge or profile of a part, face milling focuses on creating a clean, wide face. It’s often the first step in squaring up a workpiece or prepping raw stock in a facing milling machine . What makes it effective is the tool design. A face mill tool typically uses multiple cutting edges (inserts) mounted in a circular holder. These inserts do most of the work, shaving off material in fast, controlled passes. You’ll find face mills in CNC shops, manual mills, and production floors alike, especially where consistency and finish quality matter. How the Face Milling Process Works The concept is simple: a rotating face mill sweeps across the surface of your material, cutting with the edges on the bottom of the tool. The setup, however, is where the real work begins. In a typical operation, the facing mill is mounted in a vertical spindle. As it spins, the inserts take shallow bites out of the material with each pass. The machine feeds the workpiece horizontally while the tool keeps cutting, layer by layer. It’s fast, consistent, and perfect for prepping a surface for tight-tolerance parts. The results depend on your setup, feed rate, cutting speed, tool path, and depth of cut all play a role. A roughing pass might take off more material quickly, while a finishing pass uses a finer face milling cutter for that clean, reflective finish. Tool rigidity and part stability matter. If your setup flexes, the finish suffers. If your inserts are dull, you’ll get chatter and uneven cuts. It's the kind of job where details make all the difference, and a decent face milling machine won't cover for poor planning. Roughing vs Finishing Parameter Roughing Finishing Depth of Cut 2–5 mm (0.08–0.2 in) 0.2–1 mm (0.01–0.04 in) Feed Rate Higher (aggressive) Lower (controlled) Cutting Speed Moderate Higher Tool Used Indexable face mill Fly cutter / fine-tooth mill Surface Finish Coarse Smooth (low Ra value) Common Face Milling Tools There’s more than one way to flatten a surface, and the tool you pick makes a big difference on your finish, your cycle time, and your tooling cost. Let’s break down the most common options used in face milling . Tool Selection Guide: When to Use What Tool Type Best For Pros Cons Face Mill Cutter General purpose, roughing + finishing Fast, efficient, easy insert swap Higher upfront cost Shell Mill Large parts, modular setups Versatile, scalable Needs arbor and holder setup Fly Cutter Finishing small to medium surfaces Inexpensive, smooth finish Slow, can vibrate at high speeds Solid Carbide Tool Light machines, tight spaces Rigid, compact Pricey, limited insert options Types of Face Milling Operations (ResearchGate) Face milling isn’t just about plowing a tool across a block of metal. There are different ways to run the cut, and knowing the options helps you get better results, or avoid screwing things up. Conventional Face Milling This is your go-to method. The face mill cuts across the entire top of the workpiece, removing material in overlapping passes. It’s efficient and ideal for prepping flat surfaces quickly. Partial Face Milling When the workpiece is smaller or has tricky geometry, only part of the face milling cutter engages with the material. It requires a bit more care in setup to avoid deflection and uneven cuts. Climb vs. Conventional Milling In climb milling, the cutter moves in the same direction as the feed, great finish, but it needs a solid machine. Conventional milling moves against the feed direction and offers more stability for older or lightweight machines. Some facing milling machines allow switching between the two. Slotting and Contour Facing Not every job is a square block. Face mills can be used for shallow slots or contoured faces if the toolpath is planned right. Just don’t expect perfect results unless your setup is rock solid. Here’s what separates clean cuts from chewed-up messes. ● Keep your toolpath smooth—avoid sharp corners or direction changes mid-cut. ● Use coolant when possible. It extends insert life and keeps chips out of the way. ● Watch your depth of cut—too deep and you’ll get chatter, too shallow and the tool may rub instead of cut. ● Rigid setup matters more than fancy tooling. If your part moves, your surface finish suffers. And finally, picking the right tool geometry matters. The insert’s shape, rake, and edge prep can make or break your finish, especially on tricky materials. The right face mill tool , a solid setup, and a bit of know-how can take your surface finish from “rough passable” to production-ready. events.before: Home Newsroom Keep Production on Lunar New Year Holiday 2025 Keep Production on Lunar New Year Holiday 2025 Press Release Jan 13, 2025 The Lunar New Year is approaching, and we are so grateful for your support over the past year. The Lunar New Year holiday will span from January 23rd to February 4th . All CNC Machining materials will continue production during the LNY holiday, except for Steel 45#, SUS304. Spray Painting service is unavailable . Note: The build time might be 2-3 days longer than usual during the LNY holiday. During the Lunar New Year holiday, 3D printing and CNC machining orders cannot be combined for shipping, nor can they be combined with PCB/Stencil orders. This will resume on February 5th. Below is the production and shipping schedule. Please kindly schedule the order placement time properly to guarantee the timely completion of your projects. Factory & Shipping Schedule: Order Schedule for reference: Notes: · There is no shipping pickup service on Sunday, January 19th. · The 'Confirm Date' is the day when your order's manufacturing data is complete and the order is prepared for production. Verify Now Blog > Turning Student Ideas into Real Projects with the PCBWay Future Innovators Program Turning Student Ideas into Real Projects with the PCBWay Future Innovators Program by: Mila Sep 15,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News For students, turning an engineering idea into a working prototype is an important part of learning. But moving from a schematic or CAD model to a manufactured product can be challenging when budget and access to manufacturing resources are limited. The PCBWay Future Innovators Program is designed to help students and educational institutions bridge that gap. By providing manufacturing support for eligible educational and non-commercial projects, PCBWay helps students gain hands-on experience and turn their ideas into real, testable hardware. Why Hands-On Manufacturing Matters for Students Engineering education goes beyond textbooks and simulations. Designing a circuit, creating a PCB, building a mechanical enclosure, and testing a working prototype allow students to understand how engineering concepts translate into real-world products. For many student projects, however, manufacturing can become a practical challenge. Prototype costs, limited access to equipment, and the difficulty of producing small quantities may prevent students from taking a project beyond the design stage. This is where manufacturing support can make a difference. With the Future Innovators Program, eligible students can receive support for projects related to education, research, competitions, graduation projects, open-source development, and social-impact innovation. Supporting Student Projects from PCB to Prototype The program is intended to support more than just PCB fabrication. Eligible manufacturing charges can include: PCB manufacturing PCBA assembly services 3D printing CNC machining Sheet metal fabrication Other approved in-house manufacturing services This gives students more flexibility when developing complete prototypes that combine electronics, mechanical parts, and enclosures. For example, a robotics team may need a custom PCB, CNC-machined structural parts, and 3D-printed components. A student developing an IoT device may need both PCB assembly and a custom enclosure. By bringing these manufacturing capabilities together, PCBWay can help students move more efficiently from concept to physical prototype. Support for Individual Students and Schools The Future Innovators Program provides two support options based on who is purchasing and how the products will be used. Individual Student Projects Verified students working on educational, research, competition, graduation, or non-commercial maker projects can receive 50% off eligible manufacturing charges, up to USD 200 per approved project. The support is project-specific and intended for genuine student participation. Commercial production, resale, and customer-delivery orders are not eligible. School Educational Purchases Schools, departments, laboratories, and educational programs can apply for expanded support when purchasing products for classroom teaching, laboratory training, workshops, or student projects. Eligible school purchases can receive 50% off eligible manufacturing charges, up to USD 2,000 per approved purchase. This option can be particularly useful for educators who need multiple PCBs or prototype parts for laboratory exercises, teaching kits, workshops, or student training. What Types of Projects Can Apply? The program is designed around practical learning and innovation. Eligible projects can include: Course & Lab Projects — curriculum-based assignments, experiments, and engineering exercises Research Prototypes — academic research, thesis projects, and proof-of-concept development Student Competitions — robotics, electronics, automation, and engineering competitions Graduation Projects — capstone and final-year engineering projects Open-Source & Maker Projects — student-led, non-commercial projects that encourage learning and sharing Social-Impact Innovation — projects focused on environmental, accessibility, education, or community needs Classroom & Lab Batches — manufacturing support for institutional teaching and training The goal is not simply to reduce manufacturing costs, but to make it easier for students to learn by building. From Design Files to a Working Prototype A student project often develops through several stages: defining a problem, designing the solution, creating hardware, manufacturing prototypes, testing the result, and improving the design. Manufacturing is an important part of this process. A fabricated PCB can reveal layout or assembly issues that are difficult to identify from a schematic alone. A 3D-printed enclosure can expose mechanical interference. A CNC-machined part can help students evaluate fit, strength, and usability. These iterations turn manufacturing into part of the learning experience rather than simply the final step of a project. How the Future Innovators Program Works Applying for the program is designed to be straightforward: 01 — Create a Quote Prepare the relevant PCBWay quotation or order for your project. 02 — Submit Your Application Provide your student or institutional information, project details, and quote or order number. 03 — Eligibility Review PCBWay reviews student status or institutional eligibility, project purpose, feasibility, branding requirements, and other program conditions. 04 — Receive the Result Approved support is linked to the verified account and designated project. 05 — Pay & Produce After approval, pay the adjusted amount and continue with the normal manufacturing process. Approved support should normally be used within 30 days, and changes to the materials or order may require another review. Helping the Next Generation Build, Test, and Learn Innovation often starts with a simple idea: a circuit a student wants to build, a robot they want to improve, or a problem they believe they can solve. At PCBWay, we believe students should have the opportunity to take those ideas beyond the screen and into the real world. Through the PCBWay Future Innovators Program, we aim to lower some of the manufacturing barriers faced by students and educational institutions while encouraging hands-on engineering, experimentation, and innovation. Whether it is a graduation project, research prototype, competition entry, classroom project, or social-impact idea, the next great project can start with a student willing to build it. Have a student project ready to build? Explore the PCBWay Future Innovators Program and see if your project qualifies for support. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices by: Mila Sep 10,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout high speed analog to digital converter high speed adc adc layout adc pcb design High-speed analog-to-digital converter (ADC) PCB layout involves multiple design parameters, and their importance varies depending on the application. For high-speed ADC systems, the focus should not be on optimizing every routing detail, but on avoiding common design deviations and maintaining the overall performance of the signal chain. For a broader overview of PCB Layout principles, designers should also consider signal integrity, power integrity, grounding, and return paths as part of the overall design. 1. EPAD Design Guidelines for ADC PCB Design The exposed pad (EPAD), defined as Pin 0 by ADI, is the core pad located on the bottom of many integrated circuit packages. It typically provides the main grounding and thermal connection and serves as an important path for the internal ground structure. Some converters and amplifiers do not have dedicated ground pins, with their grounding function primarily relying on the EPAD. Therefore, EPAD design directly affects electrical connection stability and thermal performance and should not be overlooked in ADC PCB design. The EPAD must form a reliable solder connection with the PCB to ensure both electrical and thermal connectivity. Poor soldering or insufficient contact can lead to abnormal grounding, inadequate heat dissipation, and even malfunction of the signal chain. For reliable EPAD performance, three key aspects should be considered in ADC PCB design. Multilayer Grounding and Thermal Copper According to the device datasheet and overall thermal requirements, grounding and thermal copper structures can be added on the appropriate PCB layers. These structures should provide reliable electrical and thermal connections to the PCB ground planes, helping improve heat dissipation, particularly in high-power and multichannel signal-chain applications. The bottom layer can also incorporate a corresponding grounding or thermal area when required by the device and system design. Depending on the application, this area can support grounding, thermal management, high-frequency decoupling, or mechanical positioning for a bottom-side thermal structure. （exposed pad pcb design） EPAD Pad Segmentation A large EPAD can be divided into multiple smaller areas using a cross-hatched stencil pattern or solder mask segmentation. During reflow soldering, solder paste distribution can vary across a large continuous pad, potentially resulting in uneven soldering, voids, or insufficient effective contact. Proper EPAD segmentation helps improve solder paste distribution and create a more uniform and stable connection between the device and PCB, improving both electrical and thermal reliability. EPAD Ground Vias and Via Filling Ground vias can be added to individual EPAD sections according to the device recommendations and PCB manufacturing requirements. Whether these vias require solder paste filling, epoxy filling, or other treatment depends on the via dimensions, pad structure, and manufacturing process. For via structures that may allow solder paste to flow into the holes during reflow, appropriate via filling or solder mask treatment should be considered. This helps reduce soldering defects and improves the reliability of the EPAD electrical and thermal connection. (EPAD design: large vs segmented) 2. Power Decoupling and PDS Design for High-Speed ADC The primary goal of PCB power decoupling is to reduce the impedance of the power delivery system (PDS) to ground. A common mistake is to place large numbers of capacitors with different capacitance values without considering their actual frequency response. In practice, a large number of redundant capacitors is not always necessary. Carefully selecting capacitors based on capacitance, component type, package, and process characteristics can optimize PDS impedance while saving PCB space and reducing component cost. Redundant capacitors can introduce layout congestion, additional cost, and potential resonance risks. They do not inherently violate PCB manufacturing requirements, but excessive or poorly planned decoupling can reduce overall design efficiency. Capacitor Selection and PCB Decoupling Layout The performance of a capacitor varies with its package and construction. Even capacitors from the same supplier can have different frequency responses depending on package size, process, and component type. Therefore, there is no universal frequency limit for capacitor decoupling performance. The effective frequency range depends on package size, equivalent series inductance (ESL), component characteristics, and the actual PCB layout. If capacitor selection or placement is inappropriate, multiple capacitors can introduce additional inductive loops. Capacitors with different parameters may also resonate at specific frequencies, potentially increasing rather than reducing PDS impedance. Capacitor frequency-response characteristics should therefore be considered before placement and selection. （ADC decoupling capacitor layout） 3. High-Frequency PDS and PCB Stackup Design The effective decoupling range of discrete capacitors depends on their electrical characteristics and PCB layout, and there is no universal high-frequency cutoff. As frequency increases, package parasitics and ESL increasingly limit the high-frequency performance of discrete capacitors. At higher frequencies, the intrinsic capacitance formed between PCB power and ground planes becomes an important part of PDS design. Proper stackup design can therefore complement conventional discrete decoupling. Six-Layer PCB Stackup A typical six-layer PCB stackup can be arranged as: Top Signal → Ground 1 → Power 1 → Power 2 → Ground 2 → Bottom Signal In high-speed PCB design, keeping the dielectric thickness between adjacent power and ground planes relatively small, such as a typical range of 2–4 mil, helps increase plane capacitance and reduce the impedance of high-frequency current paths. This optimization is achieved primarily through the PCB stackup and does not require additional components. The required stackup and dielectric thickness simply need to be specified in the PCB fabrication documentation. Eight-Layer PCB Stackup Optimization For an eight-layer PCB, additional ground reference layers can be introduced while maintaining a small core-layer spacing, such as 2–3 mil. This can significantly increase the intrinsic plane capacitance, although the actual increase is not necessarily double. It depends on dielectric thickness, copper area, and the overall configuration of the power and ground layers. Compared with simply adding more high-frequency discrete capacitors, stackup optimization can reduce component count and provide a cleaner high-frequency PDS structure. PDS Impedance and Dynamic Current The primary function of the PDS is to suppress voltage fluctuations caused by the dynamic current demand of the circuit. Low-impedance power and ground planes, combined with an appropriate PCB stackup, can reduce voltage fluctuations caused by rapidly changing currents. According to V = IR, if the dynamic current is 1 A and the PDS impedance is 10 mΩ, the corresponding voltage variation is approximately 10 mV. Optimizing the PCB stackup can extend the effective high-frequency low-impedance range, but overall PDS performance is also affected by power-plane integrity, ground-via placement, package parasitics, and local current-loop design. Therefore, conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can be placed at key locations such as power-entry points, high-power devices, and surge-current devices. Combining different decoupling mechanisms can help optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. Dense capacitor placement around every IC is not always necessary and may introduce unnecessary cost, space consumption, and resonance risks. （discrete vs plane capacitance） 4. PCB Layer-to-Layer Coupling and Noise Suppression In multilayer PCB layouts, sensitive analog layers, including analog power, ground, and signal layers, can experience crosstalk when placed close to high-frequency digital layers. Because some noise sources are located directly above or below sensitive analog layers, this type of coupling can easily be overlooked. Layer Coupling in ADC Layout Adjacent PCB conductor layers form parasitic capacitive structures, which can produce electric-field coupling under certain frequency and layout conditions. The actual coupling level has no fixed value and depends on factors such as layer spacing, dielectric thickness, copper area, routing length, signal edge rate, return path, and interlayer parasitic capacitance. For example, if simulation or measurement confirms that a high-speed digital signal produces approximately 1 mV of interference at a sensitive analog node through layer coupling, this interference corresponds to about 2 LSB for a 12-bit ADC with a 2 Vpp full-scale range and about 8 LSB for a 14-bit ADC. In high-resolution ADC systems, such coupling can significantly reduce signal margin and system SNR. Therefore, during ADC layout, the signal characteristics of adjacent layers should be carefully evaluated. High-noise digital layers should be kept away from sensitive analog layers where practical, while appropriate stackup, routing, and return-path design should be used to reduce interlayer coupling. 5. Analog and Digital Grounding in ADC PCB Design In ADC PCB design, there is no universal requirement to divide the ground plane into analog ground (AGND) and digital ground (DGND). The appropriate approach depends on the device manufacturer's recommendations, system partitioning, and current return paths. In many conventional applications, a continuous ground plane is preferable to unnecessary segmentation. （Backflow Path） Why Avoid Unnecessary Ground Plane Splitting? Unnecessary ground-plane splitting can increase the inductance of current return paths. According to V = L(di/dt), higher return-path inductance increases transient voltage noise caused by rapidly changing currents and may also worsen the high-frequency impedance characteristics of the local power and ground network. As ADC sampling rates increase, switching currents can change more rapidly, making parasitic inductance in the return path increasingly important. Therefore, a continuous ground plane should generally be maintained unless system requirements indicate otherwise. Optimize ADC Return Paths Through Functional Partitioning The core of grounding design is functional partitioning and return-path optimization. By separating analog and digital circuits through appropriate component placement and controlling the return paths of high-speed digital signals, unwanted interaction between analog and digital sections can be reduced. In many applications, proper PCB layout, a continuous ground reference plane, and controlled return paths can provide good grounding performance without physically splitting the ground plane. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected at a Single Point? Ground-plane segmentation may be considered when layout constraints prevent effective functional partitioning or when high-noise digital circuits and power buses cannot be sufficiently separated from sensitive analog circuitry. However, a single-point AGND-DGND connection is not universally appropriate for every ADC system. The grounding method should be selected based on device characteristics, PCB return-path distribution, and overall system noise performance, with the device datasheet and system requirements serving as the primary references. 6. High-Speed ADC Layout Design Summary High-speed ADC layout should focus on the key factors that directly affect signal-chain performance rather than adding unnecessary design complexity. For system-level, module-level, and evaluation-board designs, a continuous ground plane can generally be preferred, with functional partitioning used to optimize return paths and reduce layer-to-layer coupling. PCB assembly processes can also directly affect system performance. Manufacturing documentation should specify EPAD segmentation, via treatment, and other relevant assembly requirements according to the device and manufacturing process to ensure reliable solder connections. Power decoupling should be based on accurate component selection and targeted placement. Combined with a PCB stackup that places power and ground planes closely together, this approach can improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can then be used at appropriate locations to optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. For high-speed analog-to-digital converter applications, ADC PCB design should be adapted to the specific system requirements. A well-planned ADC layout should focus on device connectivity, power integrity, high-frequency impedance, layer-to-layer coupling, and grounding and return paths. By addressing these factors together, designers can improve the stability and overall performance of high-speed ADC systems. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. The actual coupling level has no fixed value and depends on factors such as layer spacing, dielectric thickness, copper area, routing length, signal edge rate, return path, and interlayer parasitic capacitance. For example, if simulation or measurement confirms that a high-speed digital signal produces approximately 1 mV of interference at a sensitive analog node through layer coupling, this interference corresponds to about 2 LSB for a 12-bit ADC with a 2 Vpp full-scale range and about 8 LSB for a 14-bit ADC. In high-resolution ADC systems, such coupling can significantly reduce signal margin and system SNR. Therefore, during ADC layout, the signal characteristics of adjacent layers should be carefully evaluated. High-noise digital layers should be kept away from sensitive analog layers where practical, while appropriate stackup, routing, and return-path design should be used to reduce interlayer coupling. 5. Analog and Digital Grounding in ADC PCB Design In ADC PCB design, there is no universal requirement to divide the ground plane into analog ground (AGND) and digital ground (DGND). The appropriate approach depends on the device manufacturer's recommendations, system partitioning, and current return paths. In many conventional applications, a continuous ground plane is preferable to unnecessary segmentation. （Backflow Path） Why Avoid Unnecessary Ground Plane Splitting? Unnecessary ground-plane splitting can increase the inductance of current return paths. According to V = L(di/dt), higher return-path inductance increases transient voltage noise caused by rapidly changing currents and may also worsen the high-frequency impedance characteristics of the local power and ground network. As ADC sampling rates increase, switching currents can change more rapidly, making parasitic inductance in the return path increasingly important. Therefore, a continuous ground plane should generally be maintained unless system requirements indicate otherwise. Optimize ADC Return Paths Through Functional Partitioning The core of grounding design is functional partitioning and return-path optimization. By separating analog and digital circuits through appropriate component placement and controlling the return paths of high-speed digital signals, unwanted interaction between analog and digital sections can be reduced. In many applications, proper PCB layout, a continuous ground reference plane, and controlled return paths can provide good grounding performance without physically splitting the ground plane. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected at a Single Point? Ground-plane segmentation may be considered when layout constraints prevent effective functional partitioning or when high-noise digital circuits and power buses cannot be sufficiently separated from sensitive analog circuitry. However, a single-point AGND-DGND connection is not universally appropriate for every ADC system. The grounding method should be selected based on device characteristics, PCB return-path distribution, and overall system noise performance, with the device datasheet and system requirements serving as the primary references. 6. High-Speed ADC Layout Design Summary High-speed ADC layout should focus on the key factors that directly affect signal-chain performance rather than adding unnecessary design complexity. For system-level, module-level, and evaluation-board designs, a continuous ground plane can generally be preferred, with functional partitioning used to optimize return paths and reduce layer-to-layer coupling. PCB assembly processes can also directly affect system performance. Manufacturing documentation should specify EPAD segmentation, via treatment, and other relevant assembly requirements according to the device and manufacturing process to ensure reliable solder connections. Power decoupling should be based on accurate component selection and targeted placement. Combined with a PCB stackup that places power and ground planes closely together, this approach can improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can then be used at appropriate locations to optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. For high-speed analog-to-digital converter applications, ADC PCB design should be adapted to the specific system requirements. A well-planned ADC layout should focus on device connectivity, power integrity, high-frequency impedance, layer-to-layer coupling, and grounding and return paths. By addressing these factors together, designers can improve the stability and overall performance of high-speed ADC systems. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design by: Mila Sep 09,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout schematic design cmos pins nc pins When working on schematic design , engineers often encounter situations like this: to meet the core functional requirements, a 100-pin MCU is selected, but only 60 pins are actually used. Or a 4-channel op-amp is selected, but only three channels are needed. Some ICs may also have pins marked as NC. Seeing all those pins labeled as "Not Connected" on the schematic can be confusing. Should these unused pins simply be left floating? Should they be connected to ground? Or should they be connected to a power supply? Improper handling of unused pins can lead to undefined input states, increased power consumption, or noise interference, and in severe cases may even affect device reliability. This article explains how to properly handle these seemingly minor but important details in schematic design. 1. Why Should Unused IC Pins Be Handled Carefully? Many ICs today use CMOS technology. One key rule to remember is: do not leave CMOS inputs floating, especially digital input pins. （CMOS device） This can be understood from the internal structure of CMOS circuits. A typical CMOS input stage consists of an inverter made up of a PMOS and an NMOS connected in series. When the input is low, the PMOS is on and the NMOS is off. When the input is high, the PMOS is off and the NMOS is on. Under ideal static conditions, only a very small leakage current flows, giving CMOS circuits very low static power consumption. 2. What Happens When CMOS Pins Are Left Floating? What happens when an input is left floating? Because the input has very high impedance, it can easily be affected by surrounding electromagnetic noise, parasitic coupling, and leakage current. As a result, the input voltage may become undefined and fluctuate between low and high levels. When the input voltage falls within the transition region of the CMOS input stage, the PMOS and NMOS may both be partially turned on, causing increased supply current. In other words, floating CMOS pins have no guaranteed logic state, so it is impossible to reliably determine whether the input will be interpreted as a high or low level. 3. How to Handle Unused MCU GPIOs? Modern MCUs usually provide multifunctional GPIOs. For unused GPIOs, follow the requirements in the device datasheet and configure the corresponding IO as an output with a defined state, such as driving it low or high. If supported by the device, it can also be configured as an input with an internal pull-up or pull-down. When permitted by the device, this eliminates the need for external pull-up or pull-down resistors, saving components and PCB space. For critical pins such as interrupt, reset, and mode-selection pins, however, their default logic states should be clearly defined. Whether an external pull-up or pull-down resistor is required should be determined according to the datasheet and reference design to prevent unintended triggering. 4. How to Handle Unused Op-Amp Channels? Op-amps and ADCs require special attention because analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, and their unused pins may need to be handled differently from digital circuits. For example, if you use a dual-channel op-amp but only need one channel, what should you do with the unused channel? （IC Pins） Leaving it floating is generally not recommended because the input pins can pick up noise, causing the output to saturate and potentially increasing power consumption. What if both the non-inverting and inverting inputs are connected to ground? This puts the op-amp in an open-loop configuration, so its output may not be well controlled. For a typical voltage-feedback op-amp, if permitted by the datasheet, a better approach is to configure the unused channel as a voltage follower: connect the output to the inverting input to create negative feedback, and connect the non-inverting input to GND. However, the op-amp's input common-mode range and output swing must also be checked to ensure that this configuration is within the device's specifications. 5. What About Unused ADC Inputs? Unused ADC channels should be handled according to the device datasheet. Some devices recommend connecting unused ADC inputs to GND or another stable reference level to prevent the channel from picking up noise. However, directly connecting the input to ground should not be treated as a universal rule for all ADCs. Therefore, unused ADC inputs should not simply be treated in the same way as digital GPIOs. Always check the manufacturer's recommended connection method before finalizing the schematic design. 6. What Do NC Pins Mean on an IC? IC datasheets often contain pins marked as NC, or "No Connect." These NC pins need to be examined carefully. NC does not necessarily mean that the pin can be connected in any way. Some NC pins may have no internal connection and should simply be left floating. However, other pins marked as NC may have internal connections related to testing, reserved functions, or other circuits. The handling method must strictly follow the datasheet. For example, some datasheets specify "Must be left floating," while others specify "Must be tied to GND." If you connect NC pins to ground without checking the datasheet, you could potentially cause unexpected behavior or interfere with internal test or reserved functions. 7. The Key Rule: Always Check the Datasheet When dealing with unused IC pins, the most important principle is not simply whether a pin should be left floating or connected to ground. Instead, first identify the pin type and then follow the connection requirements specified in the datasheet. （DBV package） Different types of GPIOs, analog inputs, op-amp channels, and NC pins may require completely different handling methods. In simple terms: Unused GPIOs: Configure them to a defined state according to the datasheet. Critical input pins: Make sure they have a clearly defined default logic level. Unused op-amp channels: Use a stable negative-feedback configuration when recommended. Unused ADC inputs: Follow the device manufacturer's recommended connection method. NC pins: Strictly follow the datasheet requirements. A simple "Not Connected" label on a schematic may involve power consumption, noise, stability, and even device reliability. Do not rely on assumptions. Check the datasheet first, then decide how the pin should be connected. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide by: Mila Sep 08,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hardware design type c design usb design usb type c design usb pcb design One of the most common pitfalls in Hardware Design for Type-C interfaces is confusing the legacy protocols used by USB-A ports with the native USB Type-C protocol. Some designers mistakenly treat D+ / D− as the core charging detection pins of Type-C, which can lead to design failures. The voltage is a normal 5V, the polarity is correct, but the device still does not charge, fails to be recognized, only works in one plug orientation, or has limited charging current. Compatibility issues may also occur with some phones. In many cases, there is basically one reason: CC1 and CC2 are not connected correctly. Let's look at the most common 5V Type-C charging configuration. Once you understand it, you can use it directly in your Type C Design. 1. The Most Important Conclusion For a Type-C interface, CC1 / CC2 are the core channels for power role detection, connection detection, current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ and D− do not handle basic Type-C power detection or USB PD negotiation in a standard C-to-C connection. This is one of the key differences between traditional USB and modern USB Type C Design: CC pins: The dedicated Type-C configuration channel used for power role detection, connection detection, plug orientation detection, Type-C current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ / D− pins: Mainly used for USB 2.0 data transmission and compatibility with certain legacy charging protocols, such as BC1.2. In simple terms: C-to-C charging: Basic power detection mainly relies on CC, not D+ / D−. A-to-C charging: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may use D+ / D− for charging detection. 2. Why Does C-to-C Charging Mainly Rely on CC? Taking a standard USB-C-to-USB-C charging connection as an example, the Source and Sink first establish a connection through the CC pins. The basic process is: 1. The charger provides Rp pull-ups on CC1 and CC2. 2. The phone or other powered device uses Rd pull-downs to indicate that it is a Sink. 3. The two sides detect the connection and determine the available Type-C current capability through CC. 4. If both sides support USB PD, they can further communicate through the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. It is important to note that 56KΩ, 22KΩ, and 10KΩ Rp values correspond to different advertised current capabilities. They should not be interpreted as “56KΩ directly unlocks 5V/3A.” Therefore, Type-C current capability detection and USB PD fast charging should be distinguished: Type-C current capability detection → Rp / Rd USB PD power negotiation → PD communication over CC D+ / D− mainly handle USB 2.0 data and certain legacy charging protocols. 3. CC vs. D+ / D−: What Does Each One Actually Do? CC1 / CC2: The Core Type-C Power and Connection Pins CC stands for Configuration Channel and is an important feature that distinguishes USB Type-C from traditional USB-A interfaces. CC1 and CC2 are mainly responsible for: Power role detection: Rp indicates a Source, while Rd indicates a Sink. Connection detection: Determines whether a valid connection has been established. Plug orientation detection: The active CC pin helps determine the plug orientation. Type-C current capability detection: The Source uses Rp to advertise its power capability. USB PD communication: USB PD devices use the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. Therefore, in a standard Type-C C-to-C power connection: Correct CC configuration is critical to proper device detection and power delivery. This is why CC routing and component placement are important in USB PCB Design. D+ / D−: Data Transmission and Legacy Charging Compatibility D+ / D− are essentially USB 2.0 differential data lines. They are mainly used for: 1. USB 2.0 data transmission, programming, and communication 2. Compatibility with certain legacy USB-A charging protocols For example, USB BC1.2 charging detection mechanisms may use D+ / D−. The key distinction is: C-to-C architecture: Basic Type-C power detection relies on CC. A-to-C architecture: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may involve D+ / D−. Therefore, the fact that D+ / D− were widely used for charging detection in the USB-A era does not mean that they are required for basic charging in a USB-C-to-USB-C connection. This distinction is important in practical USB Design . 4. Three Common CC Configurations + Applicable Scenarios The most common Type-C CC configurations can be divided into three categories: Sink, Source, and DRP. Typical resistor values include: Rp = 56KΩ / 22KΩ / 10KΩ Rd = 5.1KΩ The exact configuration depends on the device role and the Type-C / USB PD requirements. Configuration 1: Dual 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → 5.1KΩ → GND CC2 → 5.1KΩ → GND Applicable to: Phones, development boards, microcontroller boards, small appliances, and other Type-C devices that work as Sink devices. Function: The device indicates that it is a powered device, allowing the Source to detect the connection and determine the plug orientation. For basic Type-C power, this configuration can support standard 5V operation. Note: Two 5.1KΩ resistors do not automatically give the device USB PD fast-charging capability. If the device needs 9V, 12V, 15V, 20V, or other USB PD voltages, an appropriate USB PD Controller and supporting power-management circuitry are normally required. （Pull-Down Resistors） Configuration 2: Dual Rp Pull-Up Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → Rp → VBUS CC2 → Rp → VBUS Applicable to: Standard USB Type-C chargers, power banks with Type-C output ports, and other devices that work as a Source. Function: The Source uses CC to advertise its power capability so that the connected Type-C device can identify the power source. Different Rp configurations correspond to different Type-C default current capabilities. They are mainly used for: 1. USB 2.0 data transmission, programming, and communication 2. Compatibility with certain legacy USB-A charging protocols For example, USB BC1.2 charging detection mechanisms may use D+ / D−.
