Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing. PCB Layout Examples: From high-speed and RF to HDI, BGA, and rigid-flex designs, we handle a wide range of complex PCB layout requirements. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Guide to Interface Driver and Connector Placement PCB Layout Guide to Interface Driver and Connector Placement by: Mila Sep 11,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout interface driver PCB connector placement interface PCB design People who design PCBs for embedded, industrial control, and communication hardware have probably heard a common PCB layout rule: interface drivers should be placed as close as possible to board-edge connectors. This is a practical guideline rather than an absolute requirement. For CAN and RS485, a slightly longer path may not immediately cause problems, while for high-speed interfaces such as USB, HDMI, and PCIe, longer traces can increase impedance discontinuities, parasitic effects, and return-path issues. If the driver is placed deep inside the board with a long trace between it and the connector, problems such as excessive radiated emissions, ESD-related MCU resets, closed high-speed eye diagrams, or communication errors may occur. This is why PCB connector placement and interface driver placement should be considered together in an interface PCB design . （Driver far from connector vs Driver close to connector ） 1. Three Common Types of Interface Drivers Interface drivers handle signal conversion and driving between the main controller on the PCB and external cables. Different interfaces have different transmission speeds, electrical standards, and communication protocols. From a functional perspective, they can be divided into three main categories. Level Translators / Interface Transceivers These devices primarily perform level conversion and interface adaptation, allowing two electrically incompatible systems on the PCB and external side to communicate correctly. RS232 transceiver (MAX232): Uses an internal charge pump to generate the positive and negative voltages required by RS-232. It converts TTL/CMOS logic levels on the MCU side into RS-232 levels, while the receiver performs the reverse conversion. RS-232 is a single-ended interface referenced to signal ground, not a differential interface. RS485/RS422 transceiver (MAX485): Converts single-ended TTL signals into differential signals and provides the drive capability required for long-distance bus transmission. CAN transceiver (TJA1050): Handles level conversion between the MCU logic side and the CAN bus, and drives and receives bus signals according to the dominant and recessive states defined by CAN. A practical CAN interface normally also requires external protection devices such as TVS diodes. High-Speed Physical Layer / PHY PHY devices for USB, Ethernet, HDMI/DisplayPort, and other high-speed interfaces integrate physical-layer functions for signal transmission and reception, including functions such as equalization and swing control. From a PCB layout perspective, controlled impedance, continuous reference planes, and an appropriate routing topology are required to maintain signal integrity. Differential impedance, such as 90Ω or 100Ω, is primarily determined by trace width, trace spacing, dielectric thickness, dielectric constant, and the reference plane. These parameters are implemented through the PCB stackup and routing design rather than being determined by the PHY itself. Differential Interface Drivers / Receivers Differential drivers and receivers such as LVDS and CML devices are used for high-speed point-to-point transmission. They precisely control differential common-mode voltage and signal swing to reduce jitter and overshoot during high-speed transmission. 2. Why Should Interface Drivers Usually Be Placed Close to Board-Edge Connectors? The following four factors apply differently depending on the interface type and should be evaluated as part of the overall interface PCB design. Shorten the Boundary Trace and Reduce EMI and ESD Risks Long traces between a connector and its driver increase the distance over which high-speed signals travel across the PCB and may increase the effective loop area of high-frequency currents. When the reference plane is discontinuous or the return path is interrupted, these traces are more likely to generate common-mode currents and additional EMI radiation. External ESD, surges, and environmental interference may also couple into the board through these paths. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens this section of the trace and reduces the high-frequency loop area, helping to lower the risk of radiated emissions and internal interference coupling. This can also reduce the workload during EMC debugging. However, EMI risk is not determined by trace length alone. Return paths, reference planes, loop area, signal edge rate, common-mode current, connector structure, and cable coupling all play important roles in PCB layout. Reduce Parasitic Effects and Maintain High-Speed Signal Integrity PCB traces inherently have parasitic capacitance and inductance. For high-speed differential interfaces such as USB, PCIe, MIPI, and HDMI, longer traces can increase the accumulated parasitic effects and make it more difficult to maintain impedance continuity. This can lead to slower signal edges, overshoot, ringing, and reflections, resulting in eye closure and increased bit error rates. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens the signal path, reduces unnecessary parasitic effects, and simplifies the routing topology, making it easier to maintain a continuous controlled-impedance transmission path. This is particularly important in high-speed interface PCB design. Shorten the ESD Discharge Path and Improve Protection Effectiveness Serial ports, Ethernet ports, and HDMI connectors are common entry points for ESD and surge energy. The effectiveness of ESD protection depends on many factors, including the type and location of the TVS device, dynamic clamping voltage, discharge path, grounding structure, PCB stackup, MCU tolerance, and interface isolation. It is therefore not determined by trace length alone. Placing the driver and ESD protection devices close to the connector and connecting them to the ground plane with short, direct traces helps provide a low-impedance discharge path. This reduces the risk of high-voltage pulses coupling into the core circuitry. During ESD testing, a system may experience MCU resets, communication errors, or, in severe cases, component damage. These problems need to be addressed through the overall protection architecture rather than relying on connector placement alone. Maintain a Continuous Path Between the Transceiver and Connector For differential interfaces such as RS485 and CAN, the relatively small signal swing makes differential transmission an important part of their noise immunity. Rather than simply assuming that the signal will experience significant amplitude loss along a long PCB trace, it is more important to consider whether the path between the transceiver and connector is short, continuous, and supported by a clear return path. Excessive trace length, too many vias, branches, and impedance discontinuities can increase parasitic effects and reflections while also increasing the possibility of external noise coupling into the signal path. Therefore, as part of good PCB connector placement, the differential path between the transceiver and connector should generally be kept as short and continuous as practical. 3. Practical PCB Layout Guidelines for Interface Circuit Guideline 1: Typical Placement Order — Connector → Protection → Filtering / Common-Mode Processing → Interface Transceiver → Controller From the board edge toward the center, a common arrangement is: Outer edge: Board-edge connector; Protection layer: TVS diodes, ceramic discharge devices, gas discharge tubes, and other ESD protection components; Filtering / common-mode layer: Common-mode chokes, ferrite beads, and filtering capacitors; Driver layer: MAX485, PHY, CAN transceivers, and other interface ICs; Core circuitry: MCU/FPGA and other main processing devices. This is a general placement approach rather than a universal rule. The actual order should be determined based on the interface standard, device datasheet, ESD current path, and EMC requirements. Ethernet, USB, CAN, RS485, and HDMI do not necessarily use the same protection and filtering structures, so the component sequence should be adapted to the specific interface PCB design. Guideline 2: Plan the Ground Plane and Return Path in the Interface Area External interfaces such as RS485, CAN, and Ethernet may require a dedicated interface ground that is isolated from the digital or analog ground on the main board. The ground structure and return path should be planned according to the isolation architecture. Avoid routing high-speed signals across reference-plane splits, which can interrupt the return path and increase radiated noise; For isolated RS485/CAN interfaces, plan the interface-side and system-side grounds according to the isolation components and isolated power architecture; When the two ground domains must be connected, select an appropriate connection method based on the isolation and EMC design, while controlling the connection location and return path to avoid unnecessary ground loops; Avoid routing signals across split regions for long distances. A good PCB layout should always consider the signal path and its corresponding return path together. Guideline 3: Treat Differential Interfaces According to Their Speed High-speed differential interfaces (USB, HDMI, LVDS, PCIe, etc.): Perform length matching according to the interface specification and device requirements, while maintaining consistent coupling within each differential pair. Key considerations include differential impedance, intra-pair skew, and reference-plane continuity. Length matching should follow the requirements of the specific interface rather than a universal numerical limit. Routing near the connector should be as straight as practical, avoiding unnecessary 90° corners and repeated bends. RS485, CAN, and similar interfaces: These interfaces generally do not require extremely strict length matching. Greater attention should be paid to topology, such as bus or star configurations, termination, return paths, and the parasitic effects of protection devices. Avoid routing unrelated signals between differential pairs to reduce crosstalk and preserve differential performance. Guideline 4: Minimize Vias in High-Speed Paths and Provide Nearby Ground Vias Keep high-speed signals on a single routing layer from the driver to the connector whenever practical, avoiding unnecessary layer transitions; If a layer transition is unavoidable, place nearby ground vias around the signal vias to provide a continuous, low-impedance return path for high-frequency currents. The exact number and spacing of ground vias should be determined based on the stackup, via dimensions, and interface speed to reduce signal distortion and radiation caused by layer transitions. 4. Conclusion Placing interface drivers close to board-edge connectors is a practical design guideline based on signal integrity (SI) and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), rather than an absolute rule that applies to every interface. In general, placing the driver close to the connector provides three main benefits: Shortens boundary traces and reduces high-frequency loop area, helping lower EMI radiation and interference coupling; Shortens high-speed signal paths, reduces parasitic effects, and makes controlled-impedance routing easier; Provides a low-impedance path for ESD discharge and reduces the risk of ESD-related interference to the main controller. Excessive trace length, too many vias, branches, and impedance discontinuities can increase parasitic effects and reflections while also increasing the possibility of external noise coupling into the signal path. Therefore, as part of good PCB connector placement, the differential path between the transceiver and connector should generally be kept as short and continuous as practical. 3. Practical PCB Layout Guidelines for Interface Circuit Guideline 1: Typical Placement Order — Connector → Protection → Filtering / Common-Mode Processing → Interface Transceiver → Controller From the board edge toward the center, a common arrangement is: Outer edge: Board-edge connector; Protection layer: TVS diodes, ceramic discharge devices, gas discharge tubes, and other ESD protection components; Filtering / common-mode layer: Common-mode chokes, ferrite beads, and filtering capacitors; Driver layer: MAX485, PHY, CAN transceivers, and other interface ICs; Core circuitry: MCU/FPGA and other main processing devices. This is a general placement approach rather than a universal rule. The actual order should be determined based on the interface standard, device datasheet, ESD current path, and EMC requirements. Ethernet, USB, CAN, RS485, and HDMI do not necessarily use the same protection and filtering structures, so the component sequence should be adapted to the specific interface PCB design. Guideline 2: Plan the Ground Plane and Return Path in the Interface Area External interfaces such as RS485, CAN, and Ethernet may require a dedicated interface ground that is isolated from the digital or analog ground on the main board. The ground structure and return path should be planned according to the isolation architecture. Avoid routing high-speed signals across reference-plane splits, which can interrupt the return path and increase radiated noise; For isolated RS485/CAN interfaces, plan the interface-side and system-side grounds according to the isolation components and isolated power architecture; When the two ground domains must be connected, select an appropriate connection method based on the isolation and EMC design, while controlling the connection location and return path to avoid unnecessary ground loops; Avoid routing signals across split regions for long distances. A good PCB layout should always consider the signal path and its corresponding return path together. Guideline 3: Treat Differential Interfaces According to Their Speed High-speed differential interfaces (USB, HDMI, LVDS, PCIe, etc.): Perform length matching according to the interface specification and device requirements, while maintaining consistent coupling within each differential pair. Key considerations include differential impedance, intra-pair skew, and reference-plane continuity. Length matching should follow the requirements of the specific interface rather than a universal numerical limit. Routing near the connector should be as straight as practical, avoiding unnecessary 90° corners and repeated bends. RS485, CAN, and similar interfaces: These interfaces generally do not require extremely strict length matching. Greater attention should be paid to topology, such as bus or star configurations, termination, return paths, and the parasitic effects of protection devices. Avoid routing unrelated signals between differential pairs to reduce crosstalk and preserve differential performance. Guideline 4: Minimize Vias in High-Speed Paths and Provide Nearby Ground Vias Keep high-speed signals on a single routing layer from the driver to the connector whenever practical, avoiding unnecessary layer transitions; If a layer transition is unavoidable, place nearby ground vias around the signal vias to provide a continuous, low-impedance return path for high-frequency currents. The exact number and spacing of ground vias should be determined based on the stackup, via dimensions, and interface speed to reduce signal distortion and radiation caused by layer transitions. 4. Conclusion Placing interface drivers close to board-edge connectors is a practical design guideline based on signal integrity (SI) and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), rather than an absolute rule that applies to every interface. In general, placing the driver close to the connector provides three main benefits: Shortens boundary traces and reduces high-frequency loop area, helping lower EMI radiation and interference coupling; Shortens high-speed signal paths, reduces parasitic effects, and makes controlled-impedance routing easier; Provides a low-impedance path for ESD discharge and reduces the risk of ESD-related interference to the main controller. Verify Now Blog > Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply design power module ir drop remote sens Many DC-DC power chips provide a Remote-Sense function. However, many designers mistake it for an optional secondary connection and wire it directly near the power module's local output. This setup effectively renders remote sampling useless. During the debugging phase, various anomalies may occur: while the local output voltage of the power module appears normal, the supply voltage at the BGA core experiences continuous droop; the power supply may exhibit audible noise, Loop Stability degradation, and severe output voltage ripple fluctuations. Remote-Sense is not a redundant line, but a Kelvin Sensing line used to measure the actual voltage at the load. The main power path carries high load currents, whereas the Force & Sense architecture ensures the Force & Sense signal paths remain isolated. Because the Force & Sense sensing line features high input impedance with minimal input bias current, it avoids the significant voltage drops present along the power delivery path, thereby measuring the load voltage more accurately. 1. Root Cause of Remote-Sense Application: DC IR Drop Modern processor core supply voltages continue to drop, with typical values around 0.8V or 0.85V, while operating currents can reach tens to hundreds of amperes. Even with wide copper traces and dense via arrays on the PCB, inherent DC resistance remains in the copper foil, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout regions along the power path. As large load currents pass through these impedances, a noticeable IR Drop occurs. For example, assume a DC-DC module has a local output voltage of 1.0V, and the total equivalent resistance of the power path from the module to an FPGA's BGA power pins is 1.5mΩ. Under a 100A load current, the voltage drop VIR Drop = I × R = 100A × 1.5mΩ = 150mV. Thus, while the local output stays at 1.0V, the actual voltage at the FPGA BGA pins drops to approximately 0.85V due to IR Drop along the copper, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout. If the sampling point is placed locally at the DC-DC output, the Feedback Loop can only detect the local 1.0V rail. The Feedback Loop remains unaware of the 0.15V lost before reaching the load. For low-voltage core supplies, the allowable voltage tolerance is tight, depending on processor, FPGA, or ASIC specifications. Such voltage degradation caused by IR Drop leads to full-load crashes, frequency throttling, and inadequate timing margins on high-speed interfaces. Remote-Sense resolves this problem: by routing the Remote-Sense sampling line directly near the load chip's power pins, the system detects the true voltage at the load. When the detected load voltage falls below the target, the Feedback Loop increases the power stage output to compensate for the IR Drop along the power delivery path. (Remote-Sense Working Principle) 2. Kelvin Remote Voltage Sensing: Force & Sense At its core, Remote-Sense relies on Kelvin Sensing principles to segregate the high-current power path from the voltage detection line. Force Power Path The power path delivers actual energy to the load and requires sufficient copper width, copper weight, and parallel vias to lower impedance. Because this pathway carries the full load current, it inevitably suffers from IR Drop. Sense Sampling Path The Force & Sense sensing line has high impedance and carries only a tiny input bias current. According to V = I × R, because the current flowing through the Force & Sense sensing line is negligible, its trace resistance creates virtually no voltage drop compared to the high-current power line. Consequently, Kelvin Sensing measures the electrical potential at the load with high accuracy. The power converter's internal Feedback Loop continuously measures the error between the sense voltage and an internal reference voltage, adjusting power delivery to compensate for PCB power losses. For ICs featuring Differential Sensing, both VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be fully connected as specified in the datasheet. Incorrectly connecting only a single sense line may cause reference errors or disable remote sampling altogether. （Kelvin Force/Sense Schematic ） 3. Remote-Sense PCB Layout Guidelines Remote-Sense is far more than a simple jumper trace. Sampling point placement, routing methods, Noise Isolation, filtering, and Multi-Load Topology configurations all impose strict constraints. Improper implementation fails to compensate for IR Drop and risks introducing high-frequency noise into the Feedback Loop, inducing output fluctuations, degraded Loop Stability, or audible squealing. VSENSE+ / VSENSE- Differential Pair Routing VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be routed using Differential Pair Routing, kept closely coupled in identical environments. Avoid placing either trace near SW Nodes, clock lines, or other noisy sources, and never run them parallel to power switching nodes over long distances. Adequate Noise Isolation is essential to prevent interference. If the two traces experience different distances to noise sources, varying Ground Plane Reference structures, or unequal surrounding copper, external interference couples unevenly into the lines. This asymmetry converts into differential-mode noise, directly corrupting the Feedback Loop. Therefore, the main objective of Differential Pair Routing is not simply maximizing line width, but ensuring both lines share a symmetrical, low-noise environment with effective Noise Isolation, minimal loop area, and a solid Ground Plane Reference. Sensing Point Placement Incorrect: Placing the Sensing Point Placement directly across the DC-DC module's local output capacitors. This neutralizes the benefits of Remote-Sense, as the controller senses only the local output while uncompensated losses persist down the line. Correct: Proper Sensing Point Placement requires connecting the lines as close as possible to the load chip's actual power pins (e.g., near the BGA power pins), adhering to the manufacturer's recommended Sensing Point Placement guidelines. Input filtering and Decoupling Capacitors must be placed as close to the chip power pins as possible to lower the high-frequency current loop impedance at the load. The core principle of Remote-Sense layout is: The sense point must represent the true voltage received by the load, not an intermediate node along the power path. Never place sense points arbitrarily along intermediate nodes or directly on power copper pour for layout convenience. Even if schematics correctly define Differential Sensing, improper Sensing Point Placement on the PCB invalidates the feature. （Remote-Sense PCB Layout） Controller-Side RC Low-Pass Filter Sense traces often traverse long PCB paths, making them vulnerable to high-frequency interference from switching SW Nodes, DDR buses, clocks, and high-speed traces. Proper Noise Isolation helps, but if high-frequency noise reaches the sensing node, it induces output jitter and degrades Loop Stability. For long sense traces or noisy environments, place an RC Low-Pass Filter near the sense pins according to datasheet recommendations to suppress coupled switching noise. Some IC manufacturers recommend an RC Low-Pass Filter consisting of tens of ohms in series and nanofarad-range capacitors. However, specific R and C parameters must strictly follow vendor datasheets and be validated through Loop Stability testing rather than using generic values. Note that an RC Low-Pass Filter introduces an additional time constant, requiring evaluation regarding its impact on loop bandwidth, Transient Response, and overall stability. Multi-Load Topology: Reference Point at Key Load When a single power rail supplies multiple BGA devices, a Multi-Load Topology must not place the sense point at a random common node or simply at the load closest to the converter. In a Multi-Load Topology, evaluate system voltage tolerances, load currents, and power path drops to position the reference point at the most voltage-sensitive load experiencing the highest drop. For example, in a chain of DC-DC -> Load A -> Load B -> Load C, if Load C has the tightest tolerance and highest line drop in this Multi-Load Topology, connect the sense reference point directly to Load C's supply pins. This ensures the loop prioritizes the voltage margin of the critical load, while closer loads are powered via the main power path without serving as feedback references. Handling Unused Remote-Sense Pins If a design does not enable Remote-Sense, do not leave the VSENSE+ and VSENSE- pins floating, as a Floating Pin Hazard will disrupt feedback control. For controllers relying on external sense inputs, a Floating Pin Hazard leaves input potentials uncontrolled, causing abnormal output voltages and potential device damage. To avoid a Floating Pin Hazard, consult the datasheet. Devices supporting local sense mode typically require connecting VSENSE+ to local VOUT+ and VSENSE- to local GND. Always follow the manufacturer's specified wiring for local sensing, as internal architectures vary. 4. Remote-Sense Cannot Replace Power Integrity / PDN Design Remote-Sense is not a substitute for proper load-side decoupling and low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN design. Remote-Sense primarily compensates for DC or low-frequency voltage losses along the power path. When a CPU, FPGA, GPU, or ASIC undergoes a fast step change, the Transient Response of the feedback loop cannot react instantaneously. During these events, Decoupling Capacitors and a low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN supply transient current and mitigate sharp voltage dips. Therefore, comprehensive Power Integrity / PDN design requires integrating multiple strategies: Low-impedance Power/GND planes with a continuous Ground Plane Reference Adequate copper width and parallel via arrays Load-side MLCC Decoupling Capacitors Bulk capacitors Optimized power routing Remote-Sense implementation High Transient Response and stable loop margins Remote-Sense, power path optimization, and Decoupling Capacitors complement each other rather than act as replacements. 5. Additional Remote-Sense Constraints and Safety Considerations If Remote-Sense is connected to a distant load without being properly configured or enabled, incorrect feedback compensation may drive the local voltage too high, triggering OVP / UVP Protection, instability, or exceeding maximum operating limits. Always consult the datasheet to confirm: Support for Remote-Sense and Differential Sensing Allowable voltage ranges for sense inputs Correct connections for local sensing mode Requirements for an RC Low-Pass Filter Optimal Sensing Point Placement Interaction between Remote-Sense and OVP / UVP Protection thresholds Maximum allowable sense trace lengths and routing layouts If the sense voltage drops excessively due to open circuits or extreme line losses, improperly configured controllers may trigger OVP / UVP Protection to prevent overvoltage damage at the local output or undervoltage failures at the load. Ultimately, Remote-Sense is not just about routing two lines to the load. It ensures the feedback loop accurately measures the actual voltage delivered to the load while maintaining reliable OVP / UVP Protection and preventing noise or parasitics from degrading system stability.l Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Why ICs Fail After Passing ESD Tests and How ESD Differs from EOS Why ICs Fail After Passing ESD Tests and How ESD Differs from EOS by: Mila Sep 14,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout ESD protection esd protection circuit Previous articles have covered key technologies related to chip ESD, including ESD diodes, power clamps, CDM mechanisms, and ESD testing procedures, with a focus on chip-level electrostatic discharge protection. However, a common problem in real-world engineering applications is that an IC may pass all standard ESD tests but still suffer damage or failure when used on an actual customer circuit board. Engineers often assume that the problem is insufficient chip-level ESD protection. However, this judgment has limitations. Not all electrical failures are caused by ESD. In many real-world applications, the underlying cause may instead be EOS (Electrical Overstress). 1. What Is EOS? EOS stands for Electrical Overstress. It refers to a condition in which an IC is subjected to voltage, current, or power stress beyond its designed safe operating limits, resulting in electrical abnormalities or physical damage. Common EOS Scenarios EOS can occur in many real-world application conditions, including: Power supply overvoltage I/O input voltage exceeding the specified limit Output short circuits Hot-plugging transients Line surge events Power supply reversal Negative voltage stress Ground bounce Abnormal power sequencing EOS is not a single standardized failure test model. Instead, it is a general term for failures caused by excessive electrical stress. Any voltage, current, or power stress that exceeds the device's designed tolerance can potentially result in EOS failure. 2. Key Differences Between EOS and ESD Both ESD and EOS can cause electrical damage to an IC, which is why they are easily confused in engineering practice. However, they differ significantly in terms of stress characteristics, duration, energy, and failure mechanisms. （Comparison of ESD and EOS Waveforms） 3. Why Can an IC Fail After Passing ESD Tests? Passing standardized HBM and CDM tests only demonstrates that an IC can withstand specific short-duration electrostatic discharge stresses under defined test conditions. It does not mean that the device can withstand every type of electrical transient that may occur in a real system. Standard ESD Tests Have Limited Coverage Standard ESD tests are designed around defined test models and conditions. They verify whether an IC's ESD protection structures and discharge paths can safely handle specified electrostatic pulses. However, these tests cannot reproduce every electrical stress that may occur after the IC is integrated into a complete circuit board. Real-World Applications Introduce Different Electrical Stress In actual circuit board applications, electrical stress may come from: Cable insertion and removal Power-on overshoot External load short circuits Surge coupling through long cables Back-EMF from motors, relays, and other inductive loads Transient ground potential rise Abnormal sequencing between multiple power domains Accidental power connection Compared with standardized ESD pulses, these events may have longer durations, higher accumulated energy, or repeated stress characteristics, resulting in different types of IC damage. The internal ESD protection circuit of an IC is primarily designed to handle short-duration electrostatic pulses. Its purpose is to establish a controlled discharge path and divert transient energy. Therefore, passing ESD tests does not mean that an IC has system-level protection against all EOS conditions. （ESD Test PASS vs Real PCB FAIL） 4. The Functional Limits of Internal ESD Protection A common misconception in system design is that an IC can withstand all external electrical disturbances simply because its pins include an ESD protection circuit. In practice, this assumption can create significant reliability risks. What Is Internal ESD Protection Designed For? The internal ESD protection structure is an important protection layer against electrostatic events. It is designed to provide a low-impedance path for short-duration ESD currents and prevent excessive voltage from reaching sensitive internal circuits. However, this protection is not intended to absorb large amounts of energy for an extended period. It should therefore not be treated as a substitute for system-level EOS protection. What Happens Under Sustained Overvoltage? For example, if an I/O pin is continuously exposed to a voltage beyond its specified operating range and the internal protection structure enters conduction, current may continue to flow into or through the IC. As the stress continues, the protection device and related circuits can generate significant heat. Depending on the electrical stress and internal current path, this may eventually cause damage to components such as: I/O protection devices Output driver circuits Power clamp structures Metal interconnects Vias PN junctions Core input circuits The actual damage location depends on the magnitude and duration of the external stress as well as the current path inside the IC. Why Board-Level Protection Is Required A key engineering principle is that internal ESD protection is primarily intended to handle short-duration electrostatic pulses, while system-level electrical stress with significant energy should be limited and protected at the board level. Common board-level protection methods include: TVS devices Series current-limiting resistors Power clamps Fuses Overcurrent protection Appropriate grounding Proper PCB layout The goal is not simply to add more protection components, but to limit the voltage, current, and energy that can reach the IC and provide a controlled path for transient energy. （Board-Level Protection + IC Internal ESD Protection） 5. Typical EOS Damage Locations and Failure Analysis EOS damage is closely related to the actual current path created by the electrical stress. Different types of stress can affect different areas of the IC: Power supply overvoltage: May damage power clamp structures, internal power circuits, metal interconnects, and thin gate-oxide devices. I/O input overvoltage: May damage I/O protection structures, input circuits, pull-up or pull-down protection structures, and core gate circuits. Output short circuit: May damage output driver circuits, metal interconnects, vias, and local diffusion regions. Negative voltage stress: May damage I/O protection structures, junction regions, and input/output circuits. Therefore, EOS failure analysis should not rely solely on the appearance of a localized burn mark. It is more important to trace the source of the electrical stress, current entry and exit paths, stress duration, and energy to identify the root cause. 6. Engineering Differences Between ESD and EOS Failure Signatures There is no absolute method for distinguishing ESD from EOS based solely on physical failure signatures. However, practical failure analysis often reveals some characteristic differences that can be used as initial clues. Common ESD failure characteristics include: Localized single-point damage Gate-oxide breakdown Abnormalities around I/O protection structures Localized PN-junction leakage Leakage or parameter changes at a single pin Common EOS failure characteristics include: More obvious thermal damage Localized melting or burning of metal Significant thermal damage to vias or metal interconnects Large-area circuit damage Abnormalities along power paths Damage to output driver circuits Simultaneous abnormalities across multiple pins or circuit nodes It is important to note that these failure signatures are only supporting evidence and should not be treated as final conclusions. Accurate differentiation between ESD and EOS failures requires comprehensive analysis of the failure scenario, electrical test data, application environment, test conditions, damage location, and physical analysis results. 7. The Risks of Misdiagnosing EOS as ESD In real-world applications, misdiagnosing an EOS failure as insufficient ESD protection can lead to an incorrect corrective strategy, wasting design resources while leaving the actual problem unresolved. When an IC is damaged by system-level EOS, simply increasing the size of the internal ESD protection structure, strengthening the internal power clamp, or widening internal metal interconnects generally cannot solve the system-level failure. The root cause may instead be related to board-level electrical stress, such as excessive external surge energy, improper TVS selection, continuous power supply overvoltage, load short circuits, abnormal hot-plug timing, or the lack of an appropriate freewheeling or clamping path for inductive loads. The key risk of misdiagnosing EOS is that engineers may continue to optimize the chip's ESD protection circuit without addressing the actual source and energy path of the system-level electrical stress. As a result, the same failure may occur repeatedly. Therefore, when investigating electrical failures in real-world applications, both chip-level and system-level factors should be considered rather than focusing only on the internal ESD structure. 8. Key Questions for Troubleshooting Suspected EOS Failures When an IC experiences an electrical failure, the following factors can be checked first to avoid automatically classifying the problem as an ESD failure: Failure Scenario Did the failure occur during a standard ESD test or during actual customer operation? Did it occur at the moment of power-up, during cable insertion or removal, after a load short circuit, or when a motor or relay was activated? Failure Location Is the problem limited to leakage at a single I/O pin, a low-resistance path between the power supply and ground, or simultaneous abnormalities across multiple pins? Has the overall operating current of the IC changed significantly? Stress Characteristics Was the failure caused by a short-duration transient pulse, continuous overvoltage, or overcurrent? Was there any periodic or repeated electrical stress or abnormal power sequencing? Board-Level Protection Does the circuit board include TVS or other surge protection? Is an appropriate current-limiting circuit provided? Does the power supply have overvoltage or clamping protection? Does the grounding path provide sufficiently low impedance? Does the inductive load have an appropriate freewheeling or clamping path? These factors can help determine whether the failure is related to system-level EOS and provide a basis for tracing the electrical stress path into the IC. Conclusion Both ESD and EOS can cause IC leakage, short circuits, functional abnormalities, and physical damage, but their stress characteristics, protection strategies, and corrective measures are significantly different. Passing standard ESD tests only verifies the IC's ability to withstand specific short-duration electrostatic pulses and does not cover every overvoltage, overcurrent, surge, hot-plugging, power reversal, or ground-bounce condition that may occur in a real system. Therefore, when investigating an IC failure in an actual application, engineers should not determine the root cause solely based on the fact that the device passed ESD testing or on the appearance of localized physical damage. Instead, the failure scenario, electrical stress, failure location, current path, board-level protection, and physical analysis results should be considered together. For electrical stress outside standard ESD test conditions, such as overvoltage, overcurrent, surge, hot-plugging, and inductive load transients, EOS should be considered as a potential root cause. Appropriate board-level protection can help limit the voltage, current, and energy reaching the IC and reduce the risk of application-level failure. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. Our customer service ready for your PCB +86-571-85317532 Electric Usagi My aim was to create a simple (no vacuum tube version) of the Usagi Electric bunny for my own personal use, PCBWay reviewed my initial order and provided important feedback so I could revise the order to achieve my ultimate goal. I appreciate the exceptional effort by the PCBWay team. My order was produced quickly and delivered quickly. The quality of the boards is excellent! This review is for the electronic board, mounted above the electronic board is a UV printed decorative board with the usagi face, mitchell Bruce Fleming Received boards were 100% Functional Fleming 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.

Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects.
